name: Aaron Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Aaron, I'm 27, and I'm field operations manager at a big vegetable grower. We do about 900 hectares of lettuce, broccoli and spring onions, almost all of it for two supermarket chains. The owner keeps a beef herd on the grass between vegetable crops, but my job is the veg. In summer I've got about 60 pickers working under me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five checking the orders that came in overnight, because the supermarket can change how much broccoli it wants by the morning. Then I plan which fields get cut, which crews go where, and what the forecast does to all of it. In the afternoon I'm out walking crops and talking to crew leaders, mostly in a mix of three languages. I love the puzzle of it, getting the right crop to the packhouse at the right size. What wears me out is the supermarket buyers, who can cancel a whole order with one email.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Noor, my partner, who's a nurse at the regional hospital. I use AI every day, for planning the crews, checking disease photos and forecasting yield. This year I talked the owner into trialling a laser weeding robot, which burns weeds without spraying. We've got about five months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd be a bit disappointed. I'm the one who keeps buying the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that didn't live up to the talk. It helps me plan crews and saves an hour a day, which is real. But the pickers are still the ones getting the broccoli out of the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved for the crews and frustrated for myself. I'd hoped the robots would take the worst jobs, the bent-over cutting in the rain. If that doesn't happen, people keep doing work that wrecks their backs by 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools I've got and push for the ones that actually work, like the weeder. I'd spend more time on the crews, maybe better shelters and pay rates for the pickers, since the tech isn't going to fix that. Noor and I would keep saving, maybe for a flat of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but a bit flat. Like a season that's fine but you don't learn anything from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pickers' backs. Is that something you see a lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. Jonas, one of my crew leaders, is 42 and he can't cut broccoli more than four hours now without his back going. I put him on driving the tractor, but there aren't enough tractor jobs for everyone like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the supermarkets behave any differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They'd still squeeze us on price and change orders overnight. AI doesn't fix that, that's about who has the power.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool that didn't live up to the talk, and it saves me about an hour a day. But the pickers are still the ones getting the broccoli out of the field.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved for the crews and frustrated for myself. I'd hoped robots would take the bent-over cutting in the rain that wrecks people's backs by 40.
S0.do: Keeps using his current AI tools and pushes for proven kit like the laser weeder. Spends more effort on pickers' shelters and pay rates, and keeps saving with Noor for a flat.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit flat, with frustration about the hard jobs that stay hard.
S0.quote: If that doesn't happen, people keep doing work that wrecks their backs by 40.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is the rare person who sees the plateau as a letdown, because he hoped machines would take the worst physical jobs. His concern for crew leader Jonas grounds that in a real person. He's clear that supermarket power is a separate problem AI won't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, that's the one I think we're already in, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is coming whether we like it or not, so let's make sure the people doing the work come out of it okay. If robots cut the lettuce, the pickers should be trained to run and fix them. I'd say that loudly, including to the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm the one who already runs the robots. The hard part is that I'd be the person deciding which crew goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the owner to buy two more weeding robots and trial a harvesting robot on the lettuce in the first year. At the same time I'd set up a training scheme, so ten of the crew learn to run and maintain them. I'd do an online course in robotics maintenance myself, in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd decide which crew goes first. How would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ones who want to learn the machines and give the rest as much notice as I can. And I'd write references for every single one. It sounds fair when I say it, but it'd be horrible on the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly for the pickers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets, mostly. They'd squeeze the savings out of us straight away and the pickers would get nothing. That's why I'd want a union in the packhouse and the fields, and I'd say so to the owner's face.

S1.say: I'd say the change is coming, so the people doing the work must come out of it okay. If robots cut the lettuce, the pickers should be trained to run and fix them.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well, because I already run the robots. The hard part is that I'd be the one deciding which crew goes first.
S1.do: Pushes the owner to buy two more weeding robots and trial a lettuce harvester in year one. Sets up a scheme to train ten pickers on the machines, does an evening robotics maintenance course himself, and backs a union in the fields.
S1.feel: Excited and guilty at the same time.
S1.quote: I'm the one who already runs the robots. The hard part is that I'd be the person deciding which crew goes first.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's progressive values and his love of new technology pull against each other here. He'd be the one bringing in the machines that replace his own crews, and he knows it. He tries to square that with training and references, and blames supermarkets for taking the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a robot dividend, meaning a share of what the machines earn paid out to everyone, starting right now. If AGI can grow and pick vegetables, there's no reason anyone should go hungry or broke. I'd say it at work, online, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job lasts a bit longer than the crews' jobs, but not much. If the AI can plan the crops and the robots can cut them, the owner doesn't need a field manager either. I'd be useful for maybe a year, setting it all up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on learning the systems in the first six months, so I'm the person who installs them across farms. I'd talk to two other growers about doing it on contract. I'd keep the five months of savings safe and not take on any debt, because two years is too short to bet the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. Like the morning a big order lands and you've got four hours to fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, as early as I could. Some of them send money home to their families, so a summer without work isn't just a gap for them. I'd try to get them their last season's pay guaranteed, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say nursing is safe for a bit longer than my job, and then she'd say, but not forever. We'd probably put off any idea of a mortgage. That's fine, we're 27, we can rent.

S2.say: I'd say we need a robot dividend, a share of what machines earn paid to everyone, starting now. If AGI can grow and pick vegetables, nobody should go hungry or broke.
S2.think: Privately I think my job lasts a bit longer than the crews' jobs, but not much. I'd be useful for maybe a year, setting the systems up.
S2.do: Spends the first six months learning the new systems so he can install them on other farms, and talks to two growers about contract work. Keeps his five months of savings untouched, takes on no debt, and postpones plans for a mortgage.
S2.feel: Anxious but wide awake, like racing to fill a big order.
S2.quote: If AGI can grow and pick vegetables, there's no reason anyone should go hungry or broke.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron moves fast even in the fast scenario, aiming to become the installer rather than the installed. His politics come out sharply as a robot dividend. He's honest that his own role only buys a year or so, and he thinks first about pickers who send money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build something. Two isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up a fair transition, with training funds and support for seasonal workers who'll lose out first. I'd join a group pushing for that and I'd write about it, because people listen to a farm manager more than an activist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is the sweet spot for someone like me. Long enough to set up a business putting robots into farms, short enough that the big companies haven't taken it all yet. I'd probably earn more than I do now, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a small company with a mechanic I know, installing and fixing farm robots, and keep my job part-time while it gets going. I'd put about half our savings into tools and a van. I'd also build a training course for pickers and offer it free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but buzzing. I'd be working too hard, and Noor would tell me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting half your savings in. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's about two and a half months of money. Noor's pay would cover the rent if it went wrong. I'd rather bet on it than wait and watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at the end of the five years, when AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then probably my company gets swallowed too, because the robots will fix themselves. I'm not stupid about that. But I'd have saved, learned a lot, and I'd be 32 with time to work out the next thing.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to set up a fair transition, with training funds and support for seasonal workers who'll lose out first. I'd join a group pushing for it and write about it.
S3.think: Privately I think five years is the sweet spot for someone like me. It's long enough to build a business putting robots into farms before the big companies take it all.
S3.do: Starts a small farm-robot installation and repair company with a mechanic in year one while keeping his job part-time. Puts about half his savings into tools and a van, and offers pickers a free training course.
S3.feel: Uneasy but energised, knowing he'd overwork.
S3.quote: I'd rather bet on it than wait and watch.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is when Aaron's risk-taking kicks in fully. He'd put half his savings into a business and lean on his partner's pay as backup. He's clear-eyed that the business might itself be swallowed by AGI, and treats it as a bridge rather than a destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career. That's a lot of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this fair, so there's no excuse. Let's spend the first five building training and support, before anyone loses their job. I'd want unions and growers sitting at the same table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could build something that lasts most of my working life. I'd also have time to make mistakes and recover. I think I'd be one of the people who gets richer from this, which is uncomfortable for someone who votes the way I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd do a part-time degree in agricultural robotics, the farm paying a share. Around year three I'd set up the robot service company properly, with Jonas and a couple of crew leaders as partners rather than staff. Noor and I would buy a small house and start thinking about children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about how much I'd end up owning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring Jonas in as a partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he knows the crops better than any engineer, and because I don't want to be the guy who got rich off his crew. If it works, it should work for them too. That's my politics, I just have to actually do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you less careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, and that's the risk. With two years you'd panic, with ten you might relax too much. I'd set myself checkpoints, like a crop plan, to keep honest.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make this fair, so there's no excuse. Spend the first five building training and support, with unions and growers at the same table.
S4.think: Privately, ten years means I could build something that lasts most of my career. I'd probably get richer from this, which is uncomfortable for someone who votes the way I do.
S4.do: Starts a part-time degree in agricultural robotics in year one with the farm sharing the cost. Sets up the robot service company properly around year three with crew leaders as partners, and buys a small house with Noor while planning children.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some unease about how much he'd end up owning.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the guy who got rich off his crew.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Aaron becomes a builder and possible winner, and that makes him uneasy about his own politics. His answer is to bring crew leaders in as partners. He's aware that more time could make him too relaxed, and plans checkpoints to guard against it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mainly because of the crews. They'd be out of work before anyone set up any support, and some of them have families depending on them in other countries. What would help is a robot dividend and a training fund that starts now, not after the jobs are gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets. Whatever happens with AI, they decide the price. If nobody fixes that, the savings from robots just go to them.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be the guy who got rich off his crew.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old field operations manager on a 900-hectare vegetable farm growing for two supermarket chains, and he uses AI every day. He leans left, worries about his 60 pickers, and blames supermarket power for squeezing everyone. He loves new technology and would move first in every scenario, from pushing robots onto the farm to starting a robot service company. The tension running through his answers is that he'd be both the one bringing in the machines and the one who wants the crews protected.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his pickers would lose work before any support was in place, and some of them support families abroad.
whatWouldHelp: A robot dividend that shares what machines earn, and a training fund for farm workers that starts before the jobs go.
